did_you_know.text: Did you know? The distress in this chapter is described as a shared cry from the people and their wives, who appealed to their fellow Jews for help.
Did you know? Some of the people asked for grain to feed their families because they had many sons and daughters and not enough food.
Did you know? Other families had to mortgage their fields, vineyards, and homes in order to obtain grain during the famine.
Did you know? Some people borrowed money to pay the tax demanded by the king and were even forced to mortgage their fields and vineyards.
Did you know? The economic hardship became so severe that children were sold into slavery; some families could not redeem their children, and their fields and vineyards passed to others.
Did you know? Nehemiah did not settle for personal anger: he consulted with himself, confronted the nobles and officials, and called a large assembly to discuss the injustice.

Did you know? Nehemiah demanded an end to the charging of interest and the accumulation of debts, and he announced that he, his relatives, and his servants would also forgive the money and grain they had lent.

Did you know? Nehemiah’s proposed solution included returning the fields, vineyards, olive groves, and homes, as well as giving up the interest on the money, grain, new wine, and olive oil that the lenders had demanded.

Did you know? After the people agreed, Nehemiah called the priests to make the committed people swear an oath, then shook out the folds of his robe as a symbol that God would shake out and empty anyone who failed to keep the commitment.

Did you know? Nehemiah served as governor for twelve years, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, and during that time he did not eat the governor’s provisions as his predecessors had done.
